articles.title: Meet Jessica Liao Mayers, who launched a swimwear brand with $300 and a sewing machine at 21; 11 years later, she sold the bootstrapped business in a seven-figure deal
articles.summary: Jessica Liao Mayers was 21 when she started Slate Swim from her home in November 2015.
articles.body: Jessica Liao Mayers was 21 when she started Slate Swim from her home in November 2015. She spent $300 on fabric and made each product to order on a sewing machine she already owned, fitting the work around her job as a buyer at the apparel company Tobi. Eleven years later, in July 2026, she completed a seven-figure acquisition of the brand, never raising outside capital. Slate’s minimalist, seamless swimwear was built on reinvested revenue and a deliberate focus on one category. Mayers now plans to launch Knitte, a contemporary minimalist womenswear brand, in spring 2027.How did Jessica Liao Mayers build Slate swimwear from $300As per an Entrepreneur interview with Jessica Liao Mayers, she saw a gap between mass-produced, thick nylon swimsuits at one end of the market and high-end, trendy brands at the other. She found nothing minimalist and started the brand partly because she had struggled to find comfortable swimwear for herself. Slate's swimsuits have minimal seaming so that they lie flat and smooth on the body, and they use a thin, soft fabric. The first fabrics she experimented with were lining fabrics, which was unusual at the time.The brand's first major step came when Agenda Trade Show found Slate's early Instagram account and invited her to exhibit. Before she had inventory or a manufacturer, Mayers made 30 samples herself in her apartment. She gave Tobi a week's notice because she had been due to attend the same show as a buyer. At the show, Slate secured 22 retailers, including Diane's Beachwear. She was introduced to a small Los Angeles production shop to fulfil the early wholesale orders and later moved production overseas to a small, family-owned manufacturer run by a contact she knew through Tobi.Jessica Liao Mayers grows Slate without outside fundingMayers never raised outside capital. Instead, she reinvested what the company earned in production, branding, photography and e-commerce, and moved carefully with inventory. She told Entrepreneur that everything grew at a slower pace but was very manageable. Slate stayed in its lane for 11 years, and Mayers resisted suggestions to expand into menswear, resortwear and other adjacent categories. In her words, she would much rather be successful at one thing than mediocre at many things.Mayers tried trend-forward colours, including neon yellow, in one collection and the products performed poorly. Early on, photographers reached out to pull suits for beach and test shoots, giving her high-quality imagery in exchange for credit and tags. One influencer's photo in a Slate piece generated 30 orders overnight, and Mayers also gifted products to people who fit the brand. Slate did not invest in advertising until 2021. According to Mayers, the business grew about 76% in its first year of paid marketing after she hired an advertising team with an engineering background. She says she would do ads sooner if she could change one thing.Jessica Liao Mayers sells Slate swimwear in a seven-figure dealSlate's model was direct-to-consumer sales and wholesale, with 92% of the business from direct-to-consumer and 8% from wholesale. Mayers says the company grew 36% year over year in its final three years under her ownership. In July 2026, she completed a seven-figure acquisition after listing the brand with an online brokerage shortly after Slate's 10th anniversary. She told Entrepreneur she was ready to pursue contemporary womenswear and wanted a buyer who would understand the business and value its identity. She found one with a swim background, fashion knowledge and strong marketing and media instincts.Slate was organised and profitable, and it relied on contractors rather than full-time salaried employees, so the deal moved quickly. Mayers says her lawyer described it as the fastest acquisition he had seen. She is staying involved to support the transition and plans to launch Knitte, a contemporary minimalist womenswear brand, in spring 2027. She advises founders to start with a genuine point of view, be resourceful, and stay committed for the long haul.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Colombian president purges National Museum of works promoting ‘communism’
articles.summary: Far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella says he will wage a ‘counterrevolution’ against cultural institutions.
articles.body:
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has announced he is spearheading a cultural “counterrevolution” that includes removing dozens of exhibits from the National Museum, drawing protests and comparisons to United States President Donald Trump.

De la Espriella, a conservative Trump ally , said last week that he wants to prevent cultural institutions from being taken over by what he calls “atheist social communism”.

Since then, exhibits have been taken down that once addressed the history of social movements, including feminist and LGBTQ activism, and Colombia’s political violence.

The changes have sparked protests by civil rights groups, artists and students who have accused the government of censorship and warned that it could erase important parts of the country’s history.

Dozens of demonstrators gathered on Wednesday outside the National Museum in downtown Bogota as riot police guarded its entrance.

“I find it outrageous that they want to erase part of our history,” said Azul Riascos, a history student.

He said the government was promoting a vision of Colombia as exclusively white, Catholic and Spanish-speaking. That image, he explained, excluded Black, Indigenous and LGBTQ communities.

Gimena Sanchez-Garzoli, director for the Andes at the Washington Office on Latin America, a research and advocacy organisation, said the Colombian government’s approach reflects a broader trend among Trump allies who are copying US political narratives and strategies.

Trump has been fiercely critical of Washington museums, particularly those tied to the Smithsonian Institution .

The White House released a report in July branding leaders of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History as radical activists and ordered signs installed outside the museum telling visitors that some exhibits are inaccurate.

Nearly three months later, those signs still haven’t been installed. The museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, told Congress that the White House report “does not fairly or accurately characterise the full body of work at the museum”.

Sanchez-Garzoli said Trump’s cooperation with allied Latin American governments on security and counternarcotics efforts also has an ideological dimension.

“These are imported narratives about terrorism and about being ‘woke’,” anthropologist Arturo Sanabria said during Wednesday’s protest, describing the Colombian government’s approach as a form of neocolonial intervention.

Colombia’s Culture Minister Paola Holguin said the government was reviewing and redesigning exhibitions and curatorial practices at other museums overseen by her ministry.

Colombia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also renamed a courtyard previously honouring an Indigenous leader, describing the change as part of the president’s campaign against “woke” ideology.

“The government is making serious efforts in a cultural battle that probably doesn’t exist,” political scientist Estefania Cardozo said outside the museum. “It is inventing one to erase identities that cannot be erased because they already exist.”

articles.title: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits
articles.summary: Judges will be given new powers to impose tougher prison punishments on offenders who refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing.
articles.body:
Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing.

The tougher sanctions, due to come into effect next year, build on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years for contempt of court.

The move is the latest bid to push killers to attend court, with the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) acknowledging that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter them if they are already behind bars.

"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.

"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences", she added.

The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, social visits could be banned for nearly a month and any prison privileges revoked for longer.

Judges will also being able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for almost three months for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing.

For criminals aged 18-20, judges will be able to impose similar restrictions but for shorter periods of time, the MoJ said.

However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.

But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves".

The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa, law graduate Zara Aleena and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa have previously advocated for changes to the laws.

All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings.

Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.

Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman OBE, said the announcement follows "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice".

She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

Lisa White, who lives in Mississippi, was arrested in Long Beach after allegedly threatening to "kill federal agents" while attempting to purchase a firearm and pepper spray, according to a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement release. Homeland Security Investigations identified White as a Florida attorney in a post announcing her arrest on X. Authorities said White asked whether specific firearms could penetrate ballistic vests, then allegedly said she would target agentsâ heads if she could not breach their armor. FBI ARRESTS PROTESTER WHO THREATENED TO KILL ICE OFFICER'S FAMILY AT NJ DETENTION CENTER PROTEST, BLANCHE SAYS HSI Gulfport special agents responded, interviewed witnesses and located and arrested White, according to the release. The investigation began Sept. 23 after an agent with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives alerted HSI to the encounter at High Caliber Guns, according to a criminal complaint obtained by the Sun Herald. White entered the store around 11:30 a.m. and told employees, "I need a gun," according to the complaint cited by the outlet. She allegedly identified herself as an activist and protester and said she wanted a firearm for protection at a protest because she believed "ICE agents are becoming crazy and wild." But White also told an employee she wanted to buy a gun to kill ICE agents, according to the complaint. While discussing the weapons, White allegedly gestured toward her torso and asked whether the guns could penetrate an agentâs body armor. If they could not, she said she would need to "hit them in the head, shoulder, arm or leg," the complaint states, according to the Sun Herald. A shop employee reportedly warned White that pointing a gun at law enforcement would likely get her killed. "If I have to die, I have to die," White responded, according to the complaint. The employee then suggested White buy pepper spray instead of a gun and directed her to a shooting range for training, the complaint states. White looked at two pistols but left empty-handed after the shop declined to complete the sale and told her she could return in two to three days, the newspaper reported. Store employees then alerted authorities, prompting the investigation. "The safety of our personnel is paramount, and HSI takes any threat against federal law enforcement officers with the utmost seriousness," HSI Gulfport Assistant Special Agent in Charge Matthew Reidell said. "We commend the vigilance of the citizens for recognizing these threats and notifying law enforcement immediately, which allowed us to intervene swiftly." ANTI-ICE AGITATOR SCREAMS âIâLL KILL YOUR WHOLE F- FAMILYâ DAY AFTER DEM GOV PRAISES âPEACEFUL PROTESTINGâ White remained in custody as agents prepared a federal charge of influencing, impeding or retaliating against a federal official by threat, ICE said. EXCLUSIVE: LA ICE DIRECTOR REVEALS OFFICERS FOLLOWED HOME, HARASSED AS POLICE FAIL TO HELP IN SANCTUARY CITY "Threats against federal law enforcement will NOT be tolerated," HSI wrote on X. "HSI will continue to investigate threats against the brave men and women who put their lives on the line every day to protect our homeland." The arrest comes as ICE reports a sharp increase in threats and attacks against its personnel. HEROIC ICE OFFICERS, STAFF MEMBER OPEN UP ON GROWING DANGERS: âAM I GOING TO DIE?' In its release, the agency cited an increase of more than 1,600% in assaults, 3,300% in vehicle attacks and 8,000% in death threats against ICE officers. It did not provide the underlying totals or comparison period. ICE said President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin have made clear that violence against law enforcement will not be tolerated, warning that people who threaten or attack officers face arrest and prosecution. articles.title: 'No Jantar Mantar protest call promise': CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das let out of Tihar jail
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: CJP's Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday after promising not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CJP's Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday after promising not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar.The two were ordered to be released after furnishing personal and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each and giving the undertaking before Special Executive Magistrate Ritu Raj, an ACP in Delhi Police."I undertake and promise not to commit any breach of peace... That we reiterate our undertaking... towards peace, law and order, public tranquillity and further we specifically state that we will not make any calls for protest at Jantar Mantar till such a time that it is de-notified," said their undertakings.They were detained after attempting to enter the barricaded Jantar Mantar protest site by climbing its gates on Oct 13 as part of their protest against SIR.The magistrate held that “further judicial custody does not appear to be necessary at this stage”, despite the investigating officer seeking a further three days of judicial custody, citing a continuing apprehension of a breach of peace.The magistrate held the risk of a breach of peace could be addressed through peace bonds and written assurances. The duo must appear at every hearing. The sureties will be verified before the next hearing on Oct 23.Prosecution led by counsel - Bhairav Dass and Prashant Prakash, argued that the duo’s statements to the court and the media were “contradictory”, and alleged that a CJP member’s media remarks while they were being taken to Tihar Jail on the previous hearing date undermined the “majesty of the SEM courts”.Advocates Abhik Chimni and Pranjal Abrol countered this with an unconditional verbal apology to the magistrate and reiterated the activists’ commitment to peace and said any protest would remain within the “four corners of Constitution”.Das and Ranka were first produced before the special executive magistrate on Oct 14 in preventive proceedings initiated by Parliament Street police over apprehensions that their conduct could disturb public tranquillity. They were sent to five days of judicial custody, extended by two days on Oct 19. The magistrate had rejected their earlier sureties, citing identification discrepancies and doubts about the sureties’ ability to ensure the activists’ presence.The duo challenged the Oct 19 order before HC, but withdrew the plea after the court advised them to await the outcome of the hearing scheduled before the magistrate.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Qatar, France call for opening of Hormuz and Gaza ceasefire implementation
articles.summary: Qatari and French leaders stress need to restore freedom of navigation in Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
Qatar and France have called for freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the implementation of the so-called ceasefire in Gaza, after the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, met French President Emmanuel Macron in Doha.

A joint statement on Wednesday said the two leaders stressed the importance of restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz “without constraints or fees”.

Qatari mediator Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi had said on Tuesday that diplomatic efforts are ongoing to de-escalate regional tensions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that “Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance.”

“The two leaders condemned Iranian military attacks against countries in the region which constitute a serious breach of international law,” according to the Qatari-French statement.

The two leaders also called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza “in accordance with the agreed arrangements”, as well as the urgent, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid “without conditions or restrictions”.

The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) said on Monday that about 1.4 million people in Gaza, roughly two-thirds of the population, face acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse.

“France and Qatar reiterated their opposition to any annexation of the West Bank and called for an end to Israeli settlement policies and settler violence,” the statement added.

On Lebanon, the two countries backed full implementation of the Trilateral Framework Agreement to restore Lebanese sovereignty, disarm Hezbollah and secure a complete Israeli withdrawal.

They also warned against a security vacuum following the end of the UN peacekeeping mission’s mandate, calling for continued international support for Lebanese authorities and armed forces.

On Syria, both countries said they were ready to jointly support stabilisation and economic recovery projects in coordination with Syrian authorities.

Beyond regional issues, Qatar and France agreed to expand defence, security and economic cooperation.

Macron’s regional tour, which also included Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, aimed to strengthen strategic and economic partnerships and support efforts to restore regional stability and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: What is the FDLR, and why does its anti-Tutsi ideology endure?
articles.summary: Four former FDLR officers reveal how its anti-Tutsi ideology took root and endured in Africa.
articles.body:
Musanze, Rwanda – The Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) was built on an ideology that cast the Tutsi as enemies, according to four of its former senior officers, who say they were taught to hate them long before the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi ethnic group.

“In our history and ideology, Tutsis are referred to as ‘snakes’,” said Anastase Munyaneza, a former FDLR major general.

“The analogy is that if a snake bites you, it injects poison and you die. Therefore, it is better to kill the snake before it bites you.”

The former officers say such ideas were reinforced through Rwanda’s political and military institutions before the 1994 genocide and persisted among those who fled into neighbouring Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), after the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) took control of Rwanda in July 1994.

More than three decades later, the FDLR remains a source of regional security concerns, with its presence in eastern DRC a major point of contention between Kigali and Kinshasa.

Al Jazeera met the four former officers, who defected from the FDLR, returned to Rwanda and underwent rehabilitation at the Mutobo demobilisation centre. Their accounts offer an insight into the origins of the group’s ideology, its development in exile, and the networks that have helped it survive.

The roots of the anti-Tutsi ideology described by the former officers stretch back decades, to a period when ethnic identities became increasingly politicised and institutionalised in Rwanda.

In November 1959, a Hutu uprising helped bring about the overthrow of Rwanda’s monarchy. The period was also marked by violent attacks on Tutsis, the killing of hundreds and the forced exile of thousands to neighbouring countries.

Before colonial rule, Hutu and Tutsi identities were shaped by social, political and economic relationships. Under Belgian rule, these distinctions were increasingly formalised. In the early 1930s, the colonial administration introduced compulsory identity cards classifying Rwandans as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa, reinforcing distinctions that became increasingly rigid.

By independence in 1962, about 120,000 people, mostly Tutsi, had fled the country. Exiles in Tanzania and Zaire who sought to return staged attacks between 1962 and 1967. According to the United Nations, each incident was followed by retaliatory killings of large numbers of Tutsi civilians in Rwanda, prompting further waves of refugees.

By the end of the 1980s, about 480,000 Rwandans were refugees. President Juvenal Habyarimana argued that population pressures and limited economic opportunities made it difficult to accommodate large numbers of returning Tutsi refugees.

In 1988, exiles in Uganda founded the RPF to secure their repatriation, according to the UN.

Lieutenant Colonel Idrissa Bizimana said the exiles who launched attacks against Rwanda were branded “Inyenzi”, meaning cockroaches.

“When the RPF attacked in 1990, we were told that the same Inyenzi had attacked the country. We grew up being taught to hate them,” he said.

Bizimana said they were also taught at school that the Tutsis had come from Ethiopia and had “ruled through hatred for 400 years”.

The former officers say these narratives were carried into the military, where they shaped how soldiers were taught to view Tutsis and their place in Rwandan society.

Major-General Munyaneza said the Tutsis were rarely found in the army because they were not welcome.

“In the army, we were taught that the Tutsi were our enemy,” he said.

He recalled that soldiers had to seek permission to marry and present their fiancees for approval. If a woman was Tutsi, permission would be denied.

The justification, he said, was that a soldier’s in-laws might visit their daughter in the barracks, potentially gaining access to sensitive military information and “passing it on to the enemy”.

The former officers say the ideology they encountered in the military was put into practice during the genocide against the Tutsis in 1994.

Munyaneza said soldiers trained members of the Interahamwe militia, which included men who had retired from, deserted, or been dismissed from the army.

The Interahamwe, the youth militia of the then-ruling National Revolutionary Movement for Development (MRND) party, participated in the massacres alongside the Presidential Guard and the army, according to the UN tribunal for Rwanda.

Bizimana said members of his battalion hated the Tutsis, and took part in the killings.

“During the genocide against the Tutsi, the battalion was actively involved in the genocide in the area where it was deployed,” he said.

The killings began after a plane carrying Rwandan President Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira was shot down over Kigali on April 6, 1994. The incident triggered approximately 100 days of systematic mass killings, according to the UN.

Radio Television Libre des Mille Collines (RTLM) broadcast messages inciting violence against the Tutsis, including calls to eliminate those described as “cockroaches”.

When the RPF took control of Rwanda in July 1994, ending the genocide, former government officials, soldiers and militiamen who had participated in the killings fled into Zaire.

In eastern Zaire, the UN refugee agency reported that former members of the Rwandan Armed Forces (ex-FAR) took effective control of refugee camps, particularly around Goma.

“That was where we resumed our military activities,” Munyaneza said.

The former soldiers and militia members continued to organise militarily in exile. Their subsequent activities and alliances helped lay the foundations for the armed movement that would become the FDLR.

Munyaneza said a decisive alliance emerged in 1998, when Congolese President Laurent-Desire Kabila fell out with his former ally Rwanda.

At the time, former Rwandan soldiers and militia members were fighting under the name Army for the Liberation of Rwanda (ALiR). They reorganised under the FDLR name in 2000.

“Kabila asked us to defeat the Tutsis who had attacked him, promising in return to help us defeat the Tutsi-led government in Rwanda,” Munyaneza said.

Munyaneza said the FDLR was officially established in May 2000 by former Rwandan army commanders and politicians. It was the latest name adopted by armed groups that had been operating in exile since 1995.

“The names changed, but the same people remained involved,” he said.

He said the group’s purpose was “to overthrow the Tutsi-led government that had defeated us”, referring to the Rwandan government established after the genocide.

The FDLR’s formation after the genocide has been central to its leaders’ attempts to distinguish the organisation from the forces that carried out the killings.

In an April 2005 interview with IRIN, a news agency affiliated with the UN, the FDLR’s then-president, Ignace Murwanashyaka, denied that the organisation as a whole had participated in the genocide.

“The FDLR is a very new movement, which appeared six years after the genocide,” he said.

Murwanashyaka did not rule out the involvement of individual members.

“If one of us is responsible for this crime, you have certainly heard the allegations, but no one can say that the entire organisation committed genocide,” he said.

The group’s leadership has also faced legal action over crimes committed in eastern DRC.

On July 13, 2012, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for FDLR military commander Sylvestre Mudacumura, charging him with nine counts of alleged war crimes committed in eastern DRC between 2009 and 2010.

In September 2015, Murwanashyaka and his deputy, Straton Musoni, were convicted by a German court for leading a foreign “terrorist” organisation and aiding war crimes committed in eastern DRC.

The former officers say the FDLR has relied on a combination of external support and revenue generated through its activities in eastern DRC.

Munyaneza said the group receives financial and logistical support from the Congolese government.

“To this day, the FDLR maintains close ties with the Congolese government,” he said.

Augustin Nshimiyimana, a former FDLR colonel who served as a brigade intelligence officer and later became responsible for external intelligence, described what he said were close operational links between the FDLR, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo groups, a broad label for local armed groups operating in eastern DRC.

“The FARDC, Wazalendo and FDLR live together, fight together, occupy the same positions and receive the same uniforms,” he said.

The FDLR also raises money through its own activities, according to Munyaneza. He listed roadblocks, taxes imposed on miners and mine owners, cannabis, timber, charcoal and elephant ivory among the group’s sources of revenue.

These alleged funding networks help explain how the FDLR has maintained its operations over decades in exile. Its access to local resources and relationships with other armed actors have also raised concerns about the links between armed groups and the exploitation of eastern DRC’s natural resources.

In July 2026, the UN Security Council sanctions committee listed FDLR leader Brigadier General Sebastien Uwimbabazi and commander Gustave Kubwayo. The listings cited activities undermining peace and security in the DRC and Kubwayo’s role in the group’s targeting of civilians, kidnapping for ransom and illegal exploitation of natural resources.

Efforts to address the FDLR have become a central part of diplomatic attempts to ease tensions between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

In February 2025, the UN Security Council called on the Congolese army to stop supporting armed groups, particularly the FDLR.

Under the United States-brokered Washington Accords, signed in 2025, Kinshasa committed to neutralising the FDLR, while Rwanda committed to lifting its defensive measures.

In July 2026, the Congolese government announced that a faction of the FDLR had signed a protocol on disarmament, demobilisation and cantonment.

Rwanda rejected the arrangement, accusing Kinshasa of attempting to evade its obligations under the Washington Accords to neutralise the group.

The agreement marked a new development in efforts to address the FDLR’s presence in eastern DRC, but its implementation and the extent to which it would lead to the group’s disarmament remained key questions.

Munyaneza said the FDLR continued to deny the genocide against the Tutsi. He argued that, although the organisation’s official political narrative was framed around removing what it described as foreign Tutsi, its underlying intentions were different.

Emilien Mpakaniye, a former FDLR lieutenant colonel who was responsible for securing financial aid at the group’s headquarters in eastern DRC in 2008, said the FDLR had also passed its ideology to Congolese armed groups it trained or allied with, describing the organisation as “a coordinator of armed groups in eastern DRC”.

The former officers’ accounts suggest that the ideology has survived through more than the continued presence of armed fighters. They describe a narrative that was taught in schools, reinforced within the military and carried into exile by men who later helped establish the FDLR.

Whether the group can be dismantled, therefore, is not only a question of disarmament. It also raises questions about the persistence of the ideology that shaped its founders, the networks that have sustained it and its influence on armed groups operating in eastern DRC.

“Officially, the organisation does not say that it intends to kill Tutsis; its political narrative is that it seeks to remove what it describes as foreign Tutsi,” Munyaneza said. “However, among FDLR officers, they know that their mission is to kill Tutsis.”

articles.title: Tigray resumes daily life amid fears of wider war
articles.summary: Mekelle’s reopening offers little relief as instability and economic hardship persist.
articles.body:
Mekelle, Ethiopia- In Mekelle, shops are reopening, and banks are resuming services, but residents remain anxious about what comes next. Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters retook the Tigray regional capital on October 4, as renewed fighting raised fears that the region’s fragile recovery could be derailed once again.

Tigray, in northern Ethiopia, is still recovering from the 2020–2022 war between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the region’s dominant political movement. For residents, the return of fighting has brought new uncertainty over jobs, education, security and the future.

Daily life resumes, but hardship remains.

Businesses and financial services are gradually reopening in Mekelle, but many households are struggling to afford necessities. Delayed salaries have left public employees struggling to cover food, rent and school costs, while years of conflict have depleted family savings.

“Things may be reopening, but that does not mean our problems are over. We still have expenses every day, and without our salaries, it is difficult to know how we will manage,” said Gebregziabher, a public servant in Mekelle.

The funding crisis has affected the wider public sector. In March, Tigray’s interim administration said it could no longer cover monthly salaries for about 137,000 civil servants because expected federal budget transfers had not arrived. In April, the regional finance bureau reported an 8.5-billion-birr (about $52,000) funding shortfall affecting salary payments and development projects.

For many residents, the reopening of businesses offers only a partial return to normality. Without reliable incomes and greater security, everyday expenses remain difficult to manage.

For students in Tigray, renewed fighting has revived fears of another interruption to their education. Many already lost valuable study time during the previous war and worry about falling further behind.

In Adigrat, Shewit, a grade 10 student, said uncertainty about classes and security had left him worried about his future.

“I have already lost so much time because of the war. I am afraid that if our education is disrupted again, I will lose another year and fall further behind,” he said.

Some university students have left Tigray for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, to seek transfers to other public universities. The Ministry of Education announced temporary placements at universities elsewhere in the country for students enrolled at institutions in Tigray. More than 5,000 returning students had applied by September 17–18, according to reporting on the ministry’s programme.

Abel, a third-year student at Axum University, travelled to Addis Ababa to request a transfer.

“I didn’t want to leave, but I also can’t keep putting my education on hold. I came to Addis to see if I can transfer to another university and continue my studies. I just want to finish what I started,” he said.

For students who have already lost years to conflict, the uncertainty means more than interrupted classes. It threatens to delay graduation and make an already difficult path to employment even harder.

Border communities fear a wider conflict

Near the Eritrean border, military movements and conflicting accounts of troop deployments have heightened fears that the fighting could spread beyond Tigray.

On October 8, The Associated Press reported claims by a commander allied with Ethiopia’s government that Eritrean troops had entered Adigrat earlier that week and Idaga Hamus the following day. The AP said it could not independently verify those accounts. The conflict-monitoring organisation ACLED separately reported Eritrean troops crossing the border at Zalambessa.

On October 13, Reuters reported that Ethiopian government forces had advanced into Zalambessa, citing people in contact with residents and other sources. The report said it remained unclear whether Eritrean troops or Tigrayan opposition fighters were still present in the town. The differing accounts underscored the difficulty of establishing control of individual towns as the fighting shifted.

The developments have unfolded amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara. On October 8, Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, accused Eritrea of sending troops as far as 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopian territory in several areas of Tigray and appealed to the United Nations Security Council to respond.

Eritrea has denied invading Ethiopian territory. Its government said Ethiopia’s accusations amounted to a declaration of war and called on the Security Council to take action against Ethiopia. The competing claims have raised fears that renewed fighting in Tigray could lead to a direct confrontation between the two neighbours.

Ethiopia and Eritrea fought on the same side during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean forces supported the federal government against the TPLF. Their deteriorating relations have added a regional dimension to the renewed conflict.

In Zalambessa, residents are watching developments with concern. One resident, who declined to be named, said the uncertainty made it difficult to know what to expect in the coming weeks.

On October 16, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, tasked with restoring public services, helping displaced people return and preparing the region for elections. The announcement followed the federal forces’ takeover of Mekelle and other major towns.

The federal government says the temporary administration will help restore stability and pave the way for elected regional leadership. The TPLF has opposed the federal advance, and it remains uncertain how effectively the new administration will operate across the region.

For residents, the immediate concerns are whether salaries will be paid, schools and health facilities will function, and displaced families will be able to return safely.

In Zalambessa, Gebrehiwot said residents knew from experience what another conflict could bring.

“People are worried because we know what war means for this area. We have already suffered enough, and nobody wants to see things reach that point again,” he said.

articles.title: UK's gaps in Arctic defence leave it open to Russian attacks, committee says
articles.summary: A report by MPs urges the UK to address capability gaps including a lack of Royal Navy warships and submarines, as Russia seeks to dominate the region.
articles.body:
The UK has "glaring gaps" in its ability to defend the Arctic region, leaving it vulnerable to potential Russian attacks, a report by MPs has warned.

The Commons Defence Committee said a shortage of Royal Navy warships and submarines was leaving the country's critical infrastructure in the High North, including undersea cables and energy supplies, exposed.

In the event of a conflict, the report added that Russia could threaten the UK's population, civilian and military infrastructure and vital supply routes across the Atlantic from the US.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said it is "clear-eyed about the threat Russia posed" and is investing heavily to protect Britain's undersea cables.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer previously warned that Russia could attack Nato by the end of the decade.

The High North - which includes the Arctic circle and areas adjacent to it - has become central to the UK's defence concerns in recent years.

Earlier this year, the MoD said Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic is now back to the same levels as the Cold War era.

In the new report, MPs highlighted a "shockingly low availability" of submarines and said there was a temporary loss in ability to operate them beneath Arctic ice.

"Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening Nato sea lanes, UK critical infrastructure and the UK's nuclear deterrent," it added.

Chair of the Defence Committee, Tan Dhesi, said: "This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage."

The work to address these gaps "cannot start soon enough," he added.

In light of uncertainty over US support for Nato, the report said the UK should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (Jef), a UK-led military coalition of northern European nations, should focus more on the High North.

An MoD spokesperson said the Jef was already "strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats".

Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said: "If Nato could be at war with Russia as soon as 2030, as the former prime minister warned, that means time is just as important as money.

"To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it's too late".

articles.title: Kuwait-flagged tanker carrying 21 Indian seafarers hit by projectile in Strait of Hormuz; all safe
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Kuwait-flagged oil product tanker carrying 21 Indian seafarers was struck by an unidentified projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Kuwait-flagged oil product tanker carrying 21 Indian seafarers was struck by an unidentified projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, with all crew members reported safe, Union minister of ports, shipping and waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said.The vessel, M/T Al Dasma, was hit on October 21, amid the ongoing Middle East tensions.The minister said in a post on X that the authorities were monitoring the situation and were in contact with the ship management company to ensure the safety of the crew."On Oct 21, Kuwait-flagged oil product tanker M/T AL DASMA, carrying 21 Indian seafarers, was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. All 21 of our Indian crew members, along with the rest of the crew are completely safe," Sonowal said."We are continuously monitoring the situation and remain in close contact with the ship management company to ensure the ongoing security and wellbeing of our seafarers," he added.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) tracked the incident at a location 11 nautical miles west of Bukha, Oman.According to Times Kuwait, the strike triggered a fire aboard the tanker, which was subsequently extinguished. The vessel remained stationary following the incident, and all crew members were reported safe.Another tanker incident in Strait of HormuzThe latest incident comes amid a series of attacks and security incidents involving commercial shipping in the Gulf region.Earlier, on October 16, crude oil tanker MT ST 3, carrying 15 Indian seafarers, was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. Sonowal had said that all Indian nationals aboard the vessel were safe and no casualties had been reported.In a separate incident on October 14, chemical tanker YARA J, carrying nine Indian seafarers, was hit by a drone at Sulina Anchorage off Romania. Sonowal had said that all 24 Indian nationals aboard the two vessels involved in the incidents were safe, with no casualties or injuries.Other incidents have also raised concerns about the safety of Indian seafarers operating in the region.The ministry of external affairs (MEA) had earlier condemned attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on October 11.The ministry had referred to tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, which was reportedly struck by a drone at Sohar Anchorage.Nine crew members were rescued, while two remained missing. Another vessel, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT VALTHERA, was struck by an unidentified projectile, causing a fire on board.All 11 Indian seafarers aboard that vessel were reported safe.India reiterates call for safe maritime passageIndia has repeatedly expressed concern over attacks on commercial vessels and merchant mariners amid the escalating conflict in the Middle East.New Delhi has described attacks on commercial shipping as "legally and morally indefensible" and emphasised the need to protect seafarers and uphold freedom of navigation.The MEA has also called for an immediate end to attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure, while stressing the importance of ensuring the "safe and unimpeded flow of maritime commerce through international waterways".The government has said it remains in contact with ship management companies to monitor incidents involving Indian seafarers and ensure their security and well-being.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea
articles.summary: Kim Yo Jong, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s powerful sister, made the announcement after visiting front-line areas where North Korean troops are reinforcing the border.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea plans to resume anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts along the heavily armed border with South Korea, leader Kim Jong Un’s sister said, reviving a psychological warfare campaign as tensions rise after land mine blasts injured three South Korean front-line soldiers. Kim Yo Jong, her brother’s top spokesperson on Washington and Seoul, made the announcement Wednesday after visiting front-line areas where North Korean troops are reinforcing the border. She renewed a threat to retaliate against any South Korean provocation aimed at the fortification work. In a follow-up statement Thursday, she said the North would place “new counter means” on alert along the border and have its loudspeakers on “standby” within days. North Korea has been adding mines, barbed-wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other fortifications to what is already one of the world’s most heavily armed borders as Kim Jong Un pushes a hard line toward Seoul. Touring the area with Marshal Pak Jong Chon, one of her brother’s top military officials, Kim Yo Jong called the fortification work a “sacred and great undertaking” supporting the leader’s policy of permanently severing ties with South Korea, which he has declared his most hostile adversary amid a broader diplomatic stalemate with Washington. “Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border,” Kim Yo Jong said, using the initials of South Korea’s formal name, the Republic of Korea. She warned that if South Korean warning shots — which Seoul says are meant to force North Korean soldiers doing fortification work back across the border — cause “actual harm to our territorial security and our service persons’ safety,” North Korean border guards “will show no mercy for the armed gangsters bereft of reason.” Asked about Kim Yo Jong’s threat to resume the loudspeaker broadcasts, South Korean Defense Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna said Thursday that Seoul would need to take “proportionate measures” in response to the North’s moves along the border but did not elaborate on what steps are being considered. North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency first reported Kim’s border visit as Tuesday, but Kim later corrected it to early Wednesday in a separate statement. Following an inspection with the U.S.-led United Nations Command, Seoul formally blamed North Korean-planted mines for the Sept. 21 border blasts and urged the North to apologize and clear its remaining mines. North Korea denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of strong retaliation if provoked. “Our military leadership underlined the need to make those rogues aware that our new firepower units have taken their firing positions,” Kim told soldiers during her visit Wednesday, reminding them of her brother’s order to make the border with the “enemy ... eternally impregnable.” South Korea’s military has said that North Korean soldiers crossed the border’s military demarcation line 50 times this year during fortification work and that it responded with warning shots and broadcasts. Kim has said that South Korea’s claims of border crossings are a “false pretext” and that its provocations have increased “beyond the red line” since the mine blasts. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman, Jin Yong-Sung, called Kim’s threats “intolerable” and ordered the military to “sternly respond” to potential provocations by the North. During this week’s border inspection, Pak accused the South of making “deliberate, premeditated and absurd” claims to shift blame over the rising tensions and threatened an “overwhelming response” to South Korean provocations. He also denied that North Korean soldiers were breaching the border during fortification work, saying, “Our army knows where our borderline is better than any others,” KCNA said. Loudspeaker broadcasts are among the Cold War-era psychological warfare tactics the two Koreas have occasionally used against each other during times of tensions. South Korea’s liberal government, led by President Lee Jae Myung, halted its broadcasts after taking office last year to improve ties with the North, which later stopped its own. Kim Jong Un in recent years has cut off all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and declared it a permanent enemy as a yearslong stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington drags on.

articles.title: Pennsylvania began draining a lake after engineers found seepage at its dam; the $5.5 million rehabilitation project could begin in 2026 or 2027
articles.summary: Pennsylvania began draining High Point Lake in Somerset County ahead of schedule after engineers found seepage at the dam’s auxiliary spillway and
articles.body: Pennsylvania began draining High Point Lake in Somerset County ahead of schedule after engineers found seepage at the dam’s auxiliary spillway and embankment. The full drawdown had originally been planned ahead of a dam rehabilitation project.According to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, the decision was brought forward as a safety precaution after a partial drawdown allowed engineers to inspect the dam in dry conditions and confirm structural concerns. Over the following six to eight weeks, depending on rainfall, the water level was expected to fall until only a small pool remained to help control sediment flowing into downstream waterways. Fishing and boating were to continue for as long as possible.What led to the early draining of High Point Lake in PennsylvaniaThe Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission announced a full drawdown of High Point Lake in Addison Township, Somerset County, in August 2025. The process was brought forward after commission engineers found seepage at the auxiliary spillway and dam embankment during a routine inspection in July.After consulting design engineers and state dam safety officials, the commission partially lowered the lake to inspect the dam under dry conditions. The inspection confirmed structural concerns, prompting officials to recommend a full drawdown as a safety precaution. The process was intended to redirect water flows away from the auxiliary spillway ahead of a major dam rehabilitation project.High Point Lake remained open for fishing and boating during drawdownWater levels at High Point Lake were expected to fall gradually over six to eight weeks, depending on local rainfall, as the drawdown began in 2025. As the process continued, the reservoir was set to shrink until only a small pool remained to help control sediment flowing into downstream waterways.The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission said the lake would remain open for fishing and boating for as long as possible during the drawdown. However, visitors were advised to use caution around muddy areas along the shoreline, lakebed, and boat launch. The drawdown was intended to address safety concerns ahead of planned rehabilitation work on the dam.Pennsylvania planned fish health checks during High Point Lake drawdownDuring the drawdown in 2025, Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission staff planned to test the health of fish in High Point Lake. If appropriate, they would also consider moving as many fish as possible to other waterways through a fish salvage operation.The commission had lifted all fishing season restrictions, size limits, and creel limits to help reduce the fish population in the lake. These measures were in place at the time of the announcement. However, the commission had not confirmed that a fish salvage operation would take place.A $5.5 million dam project aimed to address safety concerns at High Point LakeThe $5.5 million rehabilitation project for High Point Lake’s dam was in the permitting phase in 2025. The plans included building a new dam embankment and spillway to meet dam safety standards set by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection.Construction was expected to begin in autumn 2026 or spring 2027, depending on when the final permits were issued. Once work began, the project was expected to take about 1.5 years to complete.The lake’s full drawdown was brought forward as a safety precaution after engineers identified seepage and confirmed structural concerns during an inspection.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘I will come for them’: Elon Musk threatens Democrats over plans to probe his empire
articles.summary: Elon Musk has warned Democratic lawmakers against using congressional oversight powers to investigate him and his businesses.
articles.body: Elon Musk has warned Democratic lawmakers against using congressional oversight powers to investigate him and his businesses. On Wednesday, he said he would pursue those he believes are behind such efforts if Democrats gain control of either or both chambers of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections.“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” Musk wrote on X, the social media platform he owns, responding to a Politico report detailing Democrats’ plans to investigate him and his businesses, including Tesla and SpaceX.“Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets,” he added.The remarks come as Democratic lawmakers reportedly prepare to scrutinise Musk’s government role, business dealings and decisions affecting national security, should they secure a congressional majority.Musk worked with US president Donald Trump’s administration through the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which sought to reduce government spending and streamline federal operations. He left his role in late May after his 130-day tenure as a special government employee expired, returning his focus to Tesla and SpaceX.According to the US Government Accountability Office (GAO), the federal workforce contracted by about 250,000 employees during 2025. DOGE has also faced calls for investigations over its access to sensitive government data, the withholding of funds and its role in dismantling the US Agency for International Development (USAID).Democrats have additionally raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest involving Musk’s companies and their multibillion-dollar federal contracts and subsidies.“The sheer number of conflicts of interest are astounding,” representative Zoe Lofgren, the top Democrat on the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, said, according to Politico.The proposed scrutiny also extends to reports that Musk ordered a slowdown of Starlink services used by Ukraine’s military. Senator Adam Schiff called for an investigation, in a social media post he wrote, “Either the President was lying or Musk was lying, but the decision to slow down satellite speed and access has life or death consequences for Ukraine.”“This deserves a full investigation by the Senate. Elon Musk should be compelled to testify before Congress and under oath,” Schiff added.Musk has maintained that decisions on Starlink’s use ultimately rest with the US president. Meanwhile, Trump has said he did not know who was responsible for the reported slowdown, while Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was told by secretary of state Marco Rubio that the restriction would be lifted.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump administration seeks Supreme Court approval to build Big Bend wall
articles.summary: US federal judge blocked wall’s construction on Texas-Mexico border amid an ongoing legal battle.
articles.body:
The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume plans to build a border wall through the Big Bend region of West Texas, as part of its anti-immigration policy to strengthen security on the border with Mexico.

The Justice Department filed an emergency request on Wednesday asking the court to lift a federal judge’s injunction in a lower court that has halted construction while a lawsuit against the project, brought by an environmental group and other challengers, plays out.

The Department of Homeland Security plans include vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology in and around Big Bend National Park.

Big Bend has about 805km (500 miles) of border, and, according to opponents of the project who have sued the administration, accounts for about 1 percent of migrant arrests.

The lawsuit , filed by plaintiffs including the Center for Biological Diversity and a Big Bend-area river guide, seeks to preserve the landscape, protect a historic church, and challenge the federal government’s waivers of environmental and historical laws to fast-track the $1.7bn project.

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an “area of high illegal entry”, requiring additional barriers to control the border.

US District Judge Kathleen Cardone issued an injunction in El Paso on October 2 halting work “until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws,” she wrote in her order.

In a later opinion, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin.

The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone’s injunction.

The Supreme Court has not yet responded to this appeal.

“Even assuming that the secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction,” the Justice Department wrote.

In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park’s landscape and wildlife.

articles.title: At 16, Jhansi girl Kalyani Srivastava built an air conditioner for just ₹1,800; her low-cost innovation reportedly cools a room by 4-5°C in an hour without adding to electricity bills
articles.summary: India is a country where scorching summers are often a problem which make staying indoors difficult.
articles.body: India is a country where scorching summers are often a problem which make staying indoors difficult. Air conditioning is also beyond the reach of many low-income households. For families living in heat-prone rural regions, summers are a challenge to survive along with electricity bills. In 2017, a 16-year-old student from Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh, attempted to find a solution to this problem.Meet Kalyani Shrivastava, a Class 12 student at Lokamanya Tilak Inter College then, who built a low-cost cooling device. She also named it the 'Desi AC'. The reported cost of making it was just ₹1,800. Designed with affordability in mind, her innovation attracted attention for its simple construction and solar-powered operation.Who is Kalyani SrivastavaKalyani’s story caught people’s attention because she had looked beyond a school project and considered a problem affecting ordinary households. Rather than trying to replicate an expensive commercial appliance, she explored how readily available materials and basic components could be put together to create a more accessible cooling solution.How Kalyani's ₹1,800 Desi AC workedAccording to published reports, Kalyani's device used a thermocol icebox and a 12-volt DC fan. The arrangement allowed air to pass through the cooling chamber before being directed outside through an elbow-shaped outlet.Reports mentioned that the device could lower the room temperature by around 4-5°C after an hour of operation. It was also described as solar-powered, meaning it could operate without drawing electricity from the household supply when powered by an appropriate solar setup.The combination made the project particularly interesting. Conventional air conditioners required a significantly larger financial investment and consumed electricity during operation. Kalyani's design, by contrast, attempted to make cooling accessible through a much simpler arrangement.It is important to understand that the device was not equivalent to a conventional air conditioner capable of maintaining a set temperature through a refrigeration cycle. It was better understood as a low-cost cooling system that used ice and moving air to provide localised relief.An idea inspired by the heatFor Kalyani, the innovation addressed a familiar challenge in the Bundelkhand region. The summers were intense here making everyday life uncomfortable. More for people who couldn’t afford an expensive AC.“For the people of Bundelkhand, it is not possible that everyone can afford an AC, and the heat is unbearable, so I got this idea and transformed it into a reality which is being appreciated a lot,” she had said in an interview.And it was the noble thought behind the project that mattered.Kalyani's experiment offered a reminder that innovation did not always begin in a sophisticated laboratory. It could also emerge from observing a problem in one's surroundings and asking whether an existing solution could be made simpler and cheaper.Harsh Goenka praised the young innovatorHarsh Goenka, chairman of RPG Enterprises, also shared a message about her on X.He wrote, “Kalyani Srivastava, a 16 year girl from Jhansi has emerged as a saviour for heat stricken rural people. She has invented an eco-friendly air conditioner costing just Rs.1800, the cheapest in the world. Let’s encourage such talent!”Recognition from prominent business leaders helped bring the project to a wider audience, even as the practical effectiveness and scalability of the prototype remained separate questions. Her innovation also received recognition through other avenues.Reports stated that her creation was selected for a national-level model competition associated with IIT Delhi. In 2018, she was honoured under the Naari Samman initiative launched by the Uttar Pradesh government.In addition to being an innovator, she was also known for her musical talent. According to contemporary reports, she had participated in Indian Idol, reaching the third round, and had won more than 50 trophies in singing competitions held in Lucknow, Agra and Kanpur.Her ₹1,800 prototype was not a demonstrated substitute for conventional air conditioning, but it represented a resourceful attempt to make cooling more accessible. A cooling device that relies on ice, for example, would require an affordable source of ice. A solar-powered fan could reduce dependence on grid electricity, but that alone would not establish how much cooling the system could deliver throughout a long, hot day.You use AI every day. articles.title: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?
articles.summary: AI uncovered long-hidden programming flaws, triggering a rare global cyber-security response.
articles.body:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world scrambled to contain the fallout of this discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.

Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.

OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

Most people may not have heard of PHP - short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor - but they most certainly interact with it daily.

PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.

When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.

But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.

AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.

It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.

The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.

That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.

Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.

A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.

Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.

More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.

What happened after the flaws were exposed?

Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.

Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.

The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database.

"These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".

Its counterparts in the EU and Australia have also issued similar alerts.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X.

"If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.

The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz.

The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can.

"Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said.

"The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.

Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.

The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.

The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure.

"Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.

What can people do to safeguard themselves?

Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.

The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors.

"Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.

The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.

articles.title: Stately guardian of a bygone Goa, the Figueiredo mansion has a story to tell
articles.summary: The 400-year-old Figueiredo mansion in Loutolim is more than a family home—it is a living museum where centuries-old artefacts, architecture and heirlooms
articles.body: The 400-year-old Figueiredo mansion in Loutolim is more than a family home—it is a living museum where centuries-old artefacts, architecture and heirlooms preserve Goa’s multicultural heritage for future generations.Not many can claim to have a museum within the walls of their own home, but Pedro Figueiredo can. For him, the treasures housed in Loutolim’s Figueiredo mansion, his 400-year-old ancestral home, are not distant relics locked behind glass, but artefacts sourced across continents—hand-carved furniture, manuscripts and heirlooms that carry the imprint of family members across generations. In choosing preservation over abandonment, the Figueiredos have transformed their Baroque-style mansion into a repository of Goa’s history.The house traces its origins back to the 1590s, when the Figueiredo family moved from Sancoale to Loutolim following a bubonic plague outbreak. The family, originally Goan Hindus from the podiar community of Sancoale, later converted to Christianity.Pedro’s mother Fatima, who had a successful career in Lisbon, began the restoration journey after visiting her house over a decade ago. She left Portugal for good in 2016, and Pedro joined her in 2017 after completing his university education. Together, they set up a museum called Vicente Joao Figueiredo Museum and homestay, in which rooms are dedicated to family members whose careers span law, medicine, and the arts.The passage of time is visible. As one enters the main door, traditional oyster-shell shutters welcome the visitor. However, once in the hall, the visitor is greeted with art deco-style French windows. As one proceeds, four-poster beds and chamber pots transition to en suite bedrooms.“The house’s oldest section dates back to the 16th century, while an expansion undertaken in the 1790s introduced grander spaces, including a ballroom, music room, and dining hall. The higher ceilings and spacious halls reflect European influences of the period, including elements associated with Gothic architecture,” Pedro told TOI. Yet, the home carries traces of Hindu, Islamic, and Goan Catholic influences.“The house has two major courtyards, or ‘raj aangan’, similar to gardens in Muslim cultures that served as private retreats and exclusive leisure spaces for royal women. In our home, these raj aangans were where couples met during the courtship period during an arranged marriage,” he said.“There is also traditional craftsmanship and intricate tile work inspired by Islamic patterns. The furniture has a fusion of Hindu craftsmanship and Portuguese design with one set of chairs having ‘trimurthi’, palm trees, and dragons. We even have a baby Jesus miniature statue with bangles that has been sculpted in the likeness of Lord Krishna,” he said.Among Pedro’s prized possessions is a custom-made East India Company crockery set bearing the family’s coat of arms, featuring orange and gold colours alongside a lotus motif showing both the family’s Christian identity and Hindu heritage.The house also preserves links to royalty and political history with a silverware set gifted by King John V of Portugal in the 18th century, he said. The museum also displays the silk sari worn by Pedro’s grandmother, Maria de Lourdes Figueiredo, when she represented Goa in the Portuguese parliament in the 1960s.Besides a 1920s Schiedmayer piano bought from Karachi and a rare 1904 camera bought from Birmingham, the mansion also has a chest of drawers carved with intricate design, one of just three ever made.With such rich history, Pedro says the family was fortunate to have a clear succession plan that prevented disputes among multiple heirs.“Vicente Joao Figueiredo ensured that the property remained intact by leaving it to his daughter, Georgina, who dedicated her life to maintaining the mansion. She never married, claiming that no man could ever bear the weight of this house,” he said.After Georgina’s death in 2008, the responsibility passed to Pedro’s grandmother, who continued caring for the property until the next generation stepped in.Today, surrounded by bougainvilleas and a swimming pool—a modern addition—the mansion stands as a bridge between Goa’s past and present.“History survives when someone chooses to protect it. Our doors are always open to anyone eager to know more about Goa’s links with other countries, continents, and kingdoms,” said Pedro.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Goa | Silver Rate in Goa | Bank Holidays in Goa | Public Holidays in Goa | Petrol Price in GoaStay updated with the latest Goa news.
